source.title: NATO, Defence Expenditure of NATO Countries (2014–2026), published 7 July 2026
source.note: Figures for 2026 are NATO estimates. Spending is core defence expenditure in current prices and exchange rates. Personnel is peacetime military strength in thousands, excluding reserves.

countries.name: Norway
notes: Shares a 198 km land border and a sea border with Russia in the High North; NATO's main watch on the Kola Peninsula and the Northern Fleet.
Long-term plan 2025–2036 adds about NOK 600 bn over 12 years. Priorities are frigates, submarines, long-range air defence, drones and the Home Guard.
Hosts NATO's Joint Warfare Centre in Stavanger and large allied exercises such as Cold Response. Chairs NORDEFCO in 2026.
Startup entry points: FMA market signals and Doffin tenders, FFI test arenas, the Nansen programme for Ukraine (NOK 1 bn investment scheme via Investinor).

countries.name: Sweden
notes: Newest ally, joined 7 March 2024 after two centuries of non-alignment.
Strong domestic industry: Saab (Gripen, GlobalEye, Carl-Gustaf), BAE Systems Hägglunds (CV90), Kockums submarines.
Gotland is key terrain for Baltic Sea control. Sweden contributes to NATO's forward land forces in Finland.

countries.name: Finland
notes: Joined 4 April 2023 and doubled NATO's land border with Russia (about 1,340 km).
Conscript model gives a wartime strength of about 280,000 and a reserve of around 900,000.
Ministry of Defence is seen as easier for startups to approach than in larger allies. Finland ranks second in European defence-tech venture funding.

countries.name: Denmark
notes: Founding member. Controls the Danish straits, the Baltic Sea gateway, and is responsible for the defence of Greenland and the Faroe Islands.
One of the fastest budget increases in NATO since 2014 (+294% in real terms).
Pioneered the 'Danish model' of funding Ukrainian production directly. NATO will place a new signal battalion HQ in Haderslev by 2029.

countries.name: Iceland
notes: Founding member with no armed forces. Contributes through its Coast Guard, host-nation support and the Keflavík air base.
Sits in the GIUK gap, the North Atlantic choke point for Russian submarines. Allies rotate fighter jets for Icelandic air policing.

countries.name: United States
countries.agency: Department of Defense, DIU (Defense Innovation Unit)
notes: About 57% of all NATO defence spending. Provides the nuclear umbrella and most high-end enablers.
Washington is reviewing troop deployments on the eastern flank, which pushes Europe to carry more of its own defence.
FFI's LINK programme has helped about 36 Norwegian firms into the US market.

countries.name: Canada
notes: Founding member. Leads NATO's forward land forces brigade in Latvia.
Arctic ally with growing focus on North American air defence (NORAD) and the High North.

countries.name: United Kingdom
notes: Nuclear power and Europe's second-largest defence spender. Leads the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), which includes all the Nordic countries.
Norway is buying Type 26 frigates from the UK; Lithuania also joins the Norwegian–UK standardized vessel programme.
Startup entry points: UK Defence Innovation and battlefield labs. Network tip: ask Ties Klinkhamer for the right door.

countries.name: Germany
notes: Joined in 1955 (as West Germany). Europe's largest defence budget in 2026 after the debt brake was loosened for defence.
Stationing a permanent brigade in Lithuania. Buys Type 212CD submarines jointly with Norway.
Startup entry points: Cyber Innovation Hub of the Bundeswehr. Accelerators and local funds help much more here than elsewhere.

countries.name: France
notes: Founding member and independent nuclear power. Left NATO's integrated command in 1966 and returned in 2009.
Startups usually need to partner with a prime (Thales, Safran, MBDA, Naval Group). The Defence Innovation Agency (AID) is the front door.

countries.name: Netherlands
notes: Founding member and hosted the 2025 Hague summit, where allies agreed the 5% target (3.5% core plus 1.5% related).
Startup entry point: MINDbase, the defence innovation hub. Expect about 18 months; it rewards how innovative you can be.

countries.name: Belgium
notes: Founding member. Hosts NATO headquarters in Brussels and SHAPE in Mons.
Reached the 2% floor in 2026 after years near the bottom of the table.

countries.name: Luxembourg
notes: Founding member with a very small army. Invests in niche capabilities such as military satellites and transport aircraft.
Hosts the NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA) in Capellen, a buyer for multinational programmes.

countries.name: Italy
notes: Founding member and major industrial base (Leonardo, Fincantieri, MBDA Italia).
Central to NATO's southern flank and the Mediterranean.

countries.name: Portugal
notes: Founding member. The Azores (Lajes) are a key Atlantic link for transatlantic reinforcement.

countries.name: Greece
countries.agency: General Directorate for Defence Investments and Armaments
notes: Joined in 1952. Fifth highest spender as a share of GDP in 2026.
Spending is driven largely by tension with fellow ally Türkiye in the Aegean.

countries.name: Türkiye
notes: Joined in 1952. Second-largest armed forces in NATO and controls the Bosporus and Dardanelles.
Large drone industry (Baykar Bayraktar TB2, Akıncı). Hosts the 2026 NATO summit in Ankara.

countries.name: Spain
countries.agency: DGAM (Dirección General de Armamento y Material)
notes: Joined in 1982. Negotiated flexibility on the 3.5% core spending target at The Hague.
Navantia signed an undersea MoU with Kongsberg in November 2026.

countries.name: Poland
notes: Joined in 1999. Builds one of Europe's largest armies with K2 and Abrams tanks, HIMARS and K9 artillery.
Logistics hub for support to Ukraine (Rzeszów). Recommended Kongsberg's Protector RS4 weapon station for the K2PL tank.

countries.name: Czechia
countries.agency: Ministry of Defence, Armaments and Acquisition Section
notes: Joined in 1999. Led the international initiative that sourced artillery shells for Ukraine from outside Europe.

countries.name: Hungary
notes: Joined in 1999. Often diverges from allies on Ukraine policy and EU support packages.

countries.name: Estonia
notes: Joined in 2004. Spends above 5% of GDP and hosts NATO's cyber defence centre (CCDCOE) in Tallinn.
Faces repeated GPS jamming and drone incursions from Russia. Fast, startup-friendly testing culture.

countries.name: Latvia
countries.agency: State Defence Logistics and Procurement Centre
notes: Joined in 2004. Hosts the Canadian-led multinational brigade. Co-leads the drone coalition for Ukraine.
Offers tax incentives for defence innovation.

countries.name: Lithuania
notes: Joined in 2004. Highest spender as a share of GDP in NATO in 2026.
Borders Kaliningrad and Belarus and hosts a permanent German brigade. Partner in the Norway–UK standardized vessel programme.

countries.name: Romania
notes: Joined in 2004. Black Sea frontline state. Russian drones have repeatedly crossed into its airspace.

countries.name: Bulgaria
notes: Joined in 2004. Black Sea state with a large ammunition industry. Adopted the euro in 2026.

countries.name: Slovak Republic
notes: Joined in 2004. Borders Ukraine and produces artillery ammunition.

countries.name: Slovenia
notes: Joined in 2004. The only ally estimated below the 2% floor in 2026; the new government plans to exceed it.

countries.name: Albania
notes: Joined in 2009. Reopened Kuçova air base as a NATO facility.

countries.name: Croatia
notes: Joined in 2009. Reintroduced conscription in 2026.

countries.name: Montenegro
notes: Joined in 2017. Adriatic coastline with the port of Bar.

countries.name: North Macedonia
notes: Joined in 2020 after the name agreement with Greece.

context.name: Ukraine
notes: Not a NATO member. Partner through the NATO–Ukraine Council.
The world's most combat-tested defence-tech ecosystem: Brave1 grants, Brave1 Market and the Delta battle-management system.
Norway supports Ukraine through the Nansen programme and the Brave Norway cooperation.

context.name: Russia
notes: NATO's main threat according to the 2022 Strategic Concept.
Borders Norway in Finnmark. Northern Fleet based on the Kola Peninsula.

context.name: Belarus
notes: Russian ally hosting Russian forces and tactical nuclear weapons.
